title: PolarisMesh SaaS adaptor discovery and integration framing
summary: Intro/discovery between Redwood and PolarisMesh to scope a lightweight SaaS adaptor that would let PolarisMesh expose Redwood inference as a managed backend for their customers. Discussed integration patterns (hosted API vs dedicated vs private), network/topology constraints, SSO/KMS needs, QA and benchmarking plan. Agreed to run a short pilot (2 weeks) and share security pack + initial pricing outline.
topics: integration patterns: adaptor proxy vs native SDK
networking: VPC peering, transit gateway, egress policies
security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs
performance and benchmarks: latency SLOs, batching, kv cache
next_steps: Redwood to share security one-pager and SOC2 artifacts (Alyssa) - due 2029-07-24
PolarisMesh to provide sample traffic profile and top-10 prompts (Maya) - due 2029-07-25
SE to spin up a short rack-level benchmark using a representative model and share results (Derek) - due 2029-07-30
Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2029-07-29 (both teams)
Price ballpark for 2-week pilot + projected unit costs (Alyssa) - due 2029-07-26
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-07-21
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording ID: ff-record-20290721-8421

Attendees (as recorded):
- Alyssa Chen (Redwood, AE)
- Derek Moore (Redwood, SE)
- Priya Patel (Redwood, SE)
- Samir Rao (PolarisMesh, Head of Cloud)
- Maya Lopez (PolarisMesh, Integration Lead)
- Tobias Kwan (PolarisMesh, CTO)
- Hannah Reed (PolarisMesh, Security Architect)

[00:00] Alyssa Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i see folks are on, uh, roughly on time. i'll kick off with a 2-minute intro to what redwood is doing now, and then derek will walk through some integration patterns.

[00:35] Samir Rao: yeah thanks alyssa, good to meet you all. we're interested in a low-friction way to offer LLM features to our customers but we have strict network egress rules and multi-tenant isolation requirements.

[01:10] Derek Moore: cool. short background: Redwood provides hosted inference, dedicated reserved pools, and private (vpc/on-prem) deployments. for partners like you, we usually recommend either a lightweight adaptor that proxies requests to our hosted API, or a dedicated private deployment if you need full data residency. the adaptor approach is faster but has more network considerations.

[01:55] Maya Lopez: quick clarifying question — when you say adaptor, do you mean we run a sidecar inside our platform that forwards requests, or a managed SaaS connector you host?

[02:20] Derek Moore: good question. both are valid. pattern A: PolarisMesh runs a tiny connector (container or lambda) in your control plane that forwards to Redwood Hosted with per-customer keys. pattern B: Redwood runs a managed connector in our infra that your platform calls — that reduces ops for you but means holding less control over routing.

[03:02] Tobias Kwan: either way we need RBAC and SSO so our customers don't have to manage another set of creds. do you support SAML SSO and SCIM?

[03:18] Priya Patel: yes, we have SAML, OAuth flows, and SCIM for user provisioning on the enterprise tier. we also integrate with KMS for envelope encryption of customer data at rest.

[03:52] Hannah Reed: on the security side — we need SOC2 artifacts, pen test report, and details on audit logging/audit retention. also our legal team will want to see data flow diagrams for the adaptor.

[04:10] Alyssa Chen: absolutely. we'll share the security pack after the call. i'll put SOC2 + SOC3 summary, pen test redacted, and an architecture diagram showing both adaptor patterns.

[04:40] Samir Rao: great thanks. on compliance/regulatory side, some of our customers are EU-based and ask for data residency. do you offer region pinning for hosted models?

[05:00] Derek Moore: we do — we can route to region endpoints and also offer our Private deployment in a customer's VPC. there is also Dedicated if you need reserved GPUs with guaranteed throughput. tradeoffs are cost vs control.

[06:12] Maya Lopez: latency is a big one for us. most of our workloads are sub-500ms generation SOMETIMES for short responses, sometimes multi-turn chat. what's your typical p50/p95 for a 128-token prompt?

[06:30] Derek Moore: depends on model and quantization but for a medium-sized open model we typically see p50 ~120–180ms and p95 in the 300–700ms range on dedicated capacity, hosted can be similar but varies with load. if you need strict SLOs, Dedicated or Private is safer. caching/prefix KV cache helps a lot for multi-turn.

[07:15] Tobias Kwan: can you explain kv cache? our engineers called it kv-cache but i want to understand in practice.

[07:30] Priya Patel: kv cache is key-value caching of prior token states for a conversation so we don't recompute all the attention states each request which gives big latency reductions for follow-ups. it's sometimes transcribed as "k v chash" in our docs, sorry, weird transcription error i've seen.

[07:55] Samir Rao: ok makes sense. on the network side we prefer not to open wide egress from our VPC. we can do either VPC peering or a transit gateway to your endpoints, but we can't allow raw internet egress for customer data.

[08:18] Derek Moore: we support VPC peering and private endpoints. for partner adaptor pattern A, you can run the connector in your VPC and connect to Redwood Private over a private peering link. for pattern B, if you want our hosted connector, we offer a private egress arrangement but that would require dedicated capacity.

[09:05] Maya Lopez: what's the onboarding timeline for a private deployment?

[09:18] Priya Patel: typical private onboarding is 6–8 weeks for first deployment (including security review and network setup). Dedicated can be faster if you already have reserved capacity with us. adaptor/proxy integration is usually 2–4 weeks.

[10:00] Alyssa Chen: for this initial conversation i'm hearing you want a low-friction adaptor that respects VPC egress restrictions, SSO integration, and a pilot to prove latency and cost. is that fair?

[10:20] Samir Rao: yes, exactly. plus we'll need a compliance packet for our legal.

[10:40] Derek Moore: ok let's walk through a proposed pilot scope. Week 0: exchange security pack and sample traffic. Week 1: spin up adaptor in PolarisMesh staging, route to Redwood hosted with per-customer api keys, run benchmarking. Week 2: evaluate metrics, review cost estimator and decide on next steps — either move to Dedicated or set up a private peering.

[11:30] Maya Lopez: for benchmarking, we can share distribution of prompt lengths, concurrency, and typical per-customer peak qps. what's the format you prefer?

[11:40] Derek Moore: CSV or parquet with columns: timestamp, prompt_length, tokens_out, latency_target, customer_tier — anything anonymized is fine. sample top-10 prompts would help for quality checks.

[12:15] Tobias Kwan: do you support model pinning? some customers want a specific open model and a pinned version for reproducibility.

[12:28] Priya Patel: yes, model pinning/versioning is supported. you can pin to a model version and roll forward using our rollout controls or canary deploy.

[12:50] Samir Rao: cost — rough ballpark for a pilot? we want to know unit economics before committing resources.

[13:05] Alyssa Chen: for a two-week pilot with low volume (dev/staging), we usually provide a modest pilot credit and estimate cost per 1k tokens for the chosen model. i'll send a ballpark estimate after we see your sample traffic but expect to see numbers in the typical hosted ranges; dedicated pricing is a different floor due to reserved hardware.

[13:45] Hannah Reed: can you describe encryption at rest & in transit. also key manager integration with AWS KMS?

[13:58] Priya Patel: data in transit is TLS 1.3; at rest we encrypt using customer-managed keys when required via KMS integration. for Private deployments we can use your HSM/KMS. logs can be configured to redact PII and we keep audit trails for token-level ops.

[15:10] Maya Lopez: any gotchas we should be aware of integrating a connector — like authentication, rate-limiting behavior, or per-customer token separation?

[15:28] Derek Moore: rate limiting is per API key and per route. for multi-tenant setups we recommend issuing per-customer keys and mapping them internally. make sure the connector handles retries gracefully and respects backoff headers; we provide SDKs and middleware examples.

[16:00] Samir Rao: ok. a couple of technical deep-dive questions — does Redwood support batching on the connector side or is batching done entirely inside your runtime?

[16:15] Priya Patel: both. runtime-level batching is our primary approach (continuous batching in the runtime), but the connector can coalesce requests if you want small batch windows. we recommend letting the runtime handle it unless you have very specific latency batching constraints.

[17:00] Tobias Kwan: on the subject of hardware, do you publish what GPU types are used for dedicated? we have customers that care about fp16 vs int8 quantization behavior.

[17:20] Derek Moore: we publish performance profiles per model and hardware. dedicated pools can be opted for A100 vs H100 equivalent hardware in our catalog; quantization support varies by model and we can run an eval.

[18:05] Maya Lopez: what's your approach to regression monitoring and quality alerts? we need to make sure answers from new model versions don't degrade.

[18:20] Priya Patel: Redwood Optimize ties model/quantization changes to eval prompt-sets. we can set quality monitors and regression alerts; you can attach prompt sets and get drift/regression notifications.

[19:00] Samir Rao: great. let's talk about SLA and fallbacks — if your hosted region has an outage, do you have automated fallbacks to other regions or model variants?

[19:18] Derek Moore: yes, smart routing can failover by policy — region fallback or model-variant fallback (e.g., smaller quantized variant). we can configure automatic fallback for partner traffic, but there are consistency tradeoffs.

[20:05] Maya Lopez: one operational question: we've seen connectors leak metadata in logs; can you confirm what you retain and for how long?

[20:20] Priya Patel: we keep request/response metadata for debugging and cost attribution. request payloads are not retained by default for hosted but can be configured. retention windows are configurable up to enterprise retention periods. we'll include that in the security pack.

[21:00] Alyssa Chen: quick aside — are there any internal stakeholders we should loop in for the pilot? product managers, infra, or legal?

[21:12] Maya Lopez: yes product and legal for sure. i'll loop in our PM and legal once we have the security docs.

[21:35] Samir Rao: on timelines, our customers want to launch an initial integration trial within August. is that feasible?

[21:48] Alyssa Chen: timeline's tight but feasible: exchange security and traffic samples this week, pilot kickoff late July / early August, two-week pilot -> decision mid-August.

[22:25] Tobias Kwan: can we get a small demo or runbook for the adaptor? a docker image and sample helm chart would help our infra team.

[22:40] Derek Moore: yes we'll share a starter repo with a dockerized connector, helm chart snippet, and SDK examples. also a troubleshooting runbook for common auth/network issues.

[23:10] Maya Lopez: about failure modes — if the adaptor loses connectivity to Redwood, what should happen? queue? fail-open? fail-close?

[23:28] Priya Patel: we advise fail-closed for sensitive data (return 503 and log) and provide configurable queueing for non-sensitive workloads. we can discuss policy per-customer.

[24:05] Samir Rao: good. we'll probably want to run a short load test with 30-minute ramp to see how caching and batching behave.

[24:18] Derek Moore: great, we can help run that with our SE team. we'll also instrument the run with token breakdowns and latency by route.

[25:00] Maya Lopez: any considerations for multi-region routing — we have EU + US customers and want local routing for residency and latency.

[25:15] Derek Moore: you can configure per-customer region routing in the adaptor mapping. for hosted you pick an endpoint per region; for private you run instances in-region and route locally.

[26:00] Hannah Reed: legal will ask about subprocessors — do you list third parties and storage locations?

[26:12] Alyssa Chen: yes we have a subprocessors list and data residency tables, we'll include that in the pack.

[26:40] Samir Rao: ok i want to circle back to cost modeling. if we expect a steady 50 qps across 100 customers for 128-token average per request, what's a ballpark monthly ingestion?

[26:58] Derek Moore: we'll need exact token math but rough calc: 50 qps * 3600s * 24 * 30 ~ 129,600,000 requests per month — wait that's requests, sorry, i did math wrong — let's do tokens per second: 50 qps * 128 tokens = 6,400 tokens/sec * 86,400 = 552,960,000 tokens/day * 30 ~ 16.5B tokens/month — that seems very high, maybe your qps is per customer?

[27:35] Samir Rao: ah sorry that's aggregate across platform. we need to refine and give you accurate traffic.

[27:50] Derek Moore: yeah please send anonymized traffic so we can provide a clearer estimate.

[28:20] Maya Lopez: any recommended models for summarization vs chat vs embeddings? we plan to offer both as features.

[28:35] Priya Patel: we suggest different model classes: smaller quantized for embeddings, medium-size for summarization, larger for open-chat. Redwood's model catalog maps workload types to recommended models and quantization profiles.

[29:05] Tobias Kwan: can the adaptor do per-customer billing tagging so we can attribute costs?

[29:18] Derek Moore: yes, we'll pass tenant headers and provide token-level cost breakout in the console and via reporting APIs.

[30:00] Maya Lopez: let's talk about success criteria for the pilot — what metrics should we agree on?

[30:12] Alyssa Chen: proposed success criteria: p95 latency < 800ms for target prompts, error rate < 0.5%, cost per 1k tokens within X% of projection, no major security gaps found by Polaris legal.

[30:55] Samir Rao: agreeable. also we want quality checks — acceptability threshold on a manual sample set (>= 85% pass).

[31:10] Alyssa Chen: can you share a 50-sample prompt set for us to run quality checks?

[31:20] Maya Lopez: yes we'll grab top customer prompts and send them.

[31:45] Derek Moore: one more technical note — if you run the connector in the customer's network, you can opt-in to send masked request bodies to our logs for debugging; otherwise we can rely on metadata.

[32:10] Hannah Reed: we won't send raw PII. masking is a must.

[32:40] Maya Lopez: what's the typical cost delta between hosted and dedicated? our buyers want to see rough numbers.

[32:55] Alyssa Chen: hosted has pay-as-you-go pricing; dedicated has a lower per-token floor but requires committed spend. we'll provide a range and show crossover points for your traffic profile.

[33:40] Samir Rao: okay, sounds good. any final technical clarifications?

[33:55] Tobias Kwan: how do you handle model updates that might break deterministic behavior? we need version locking and alerting on changes that cause regressions.

[34:12] Priya Patel: model pinning plus rollout controls and automatic quality regression alerts. we'll set up evals tied to your prompt set and run comparisons on new versions.

[35:00] Maya Lopez: what about metrics export — do you integrate with prometheus or datadog?

[35:12] Derek Moore: yes, we export metrics and traces; we have datadog, prometheus, and open telemetry support.

[35:45] Alyssa Chen: i'll summarize: redwood sends security pack & subprocessors, starter repo with adaptor + helm, and pilot pricing. polaris sends traffic profile + prompt set. se team runs bench and shares results. agreed?

[36:10] Maya Lopez: agreed.

[36:25] Samir Rao: agreed on our side, will loop in legal after we get security docs.

[36:40] Derek Moore: for the bench i'll run a small rack-level test against a medium open model and share p50/p95 and token breakdowns.

[37:05] Priya Patel: and i'll include an architecture diagram for both adaptor patterns so your infra can pick which one maps best.

[37:30] Maya Lopez: do you have any references or partner case studies for this adaptor pattern?

[37:42] Alyssa Chen: yes, we'll send a short case study about a partner that used the adaptor and scaled to dedicated later; i'll include metrics and a short timeline.

[38:10] Samir Rao: what about support SLAs during pilot? we might need a higher touch SE on call while we ramp.

[38:25] Alyssa Chen: we'll provide SE hours as part of the pilot and a named CSM for escalation.

[38:55] Maya Lopez: ok that's helpful. i have one final question on data retention for debug logs — is it possible to have logs automatically redacted and then retain for 30 days only?

[39:12] Priya Patel: yes, configurable retention windows and auto-redaction rules exist; we'll capture the exact config in the security doc.

[39:40] Tobias Kwan: timeline recap?

[39:50] Alyssa Chen: share security pack and starter repo by 2029-07-24, polaris sends traffic + prompts by 2029-07-25, se bench results by 2029-07-30, pilot kickoff week of 2029-07-29, pilot run ~2 weeks.

[40:20] Maya Lopez: that works.

[40:45] Samir Rao: thanks everyone. one last logistical question — who is the day-to-day SE contact for bench ops?

[40:55] Derek Moore: that's me, derek.moore@redwood.example (note: demo address).

[41:12] Maya Lopez: ok derek, we'll include you in the traffic sample.

[41:30] Alyssa Chen: any blockers from polaris side?

[41:40] Maya Lopez: none right now beyond legal review.

[41:55] Samir Rao: thanks. we'll get the traffic and prompts over.

[42:15] Alyssa Chen: perfect — i'll send notes and next steps after the call. anything else?

[42:35] Hannah Reed: not from security beyond the standard items.

[42:55] Tobias Kwan: no, thanks.

[43:10] Alyssa Chen: wrap up then — thanks all, speak soon.

[43:20] -- End of recording --
